Cancel closes an active preview request. In chat, a tool preview=true result is displayed in a transient local screen.

PDF, PNG and JPEG input is supported by the document preview endpoint when the configured service has document ingestion enabled. Files are limited to 8,000,000 bytes and eight pages, with additional image-pixel, OCR-word and text limits. Document input always needs the review opt-in above. The default output is .txt. The tool sends the file bytes directly to the configured NLP service without reading the file into the chat. It does not parse documents locally.

Default document output is an OCR text draft. OCR can omit or change identifiers and clinical text, including entire blank-recognition pages. Compare the draft with every source page before sharing. Document results retain complete=false, source_content_completeness=unverified and recognized_text_complete=true: the last flag describes processing of recognized text only. Failures or incomplete recognized-text processing produce no file. The original document is unchanged, including its metadata and text layers.

For a binary mask draft, use export_format="pdf" with PDF input and a .pdf output path, or export_format="png" with PNG/JPEG input and a .png output path. These exports require method="mask". The service burns padded whole-word masks into fresh page images and returns an image-only PDF or lossless PNG, and reports that it copied no source metadata or searchable text layer and verified the decoded pixels. The Agent does not re-check pixels itself. It checks the returned byte hash, format, page geometry and mask receipt against the OCR map before saving up to 32 MB atomically with owner-only access. These checks do not establish that OCR or identifier detection found everything.

Use ocr_languages=["de"], ["en"] or ["de", "en"] (the default) to select OCR packs. This is separate from language/lang, which controls privacy routing. The /privacy screen exposes both language controls and an output-format selector. Its text area is an OCR text preview, including when binary export is selected. “Save review draft” writes the returned binary after checking the source path, bytes and format again, without another service call. “Open saved file” checks that the file still matches the saved hash and opens it in the system viewer. Inspect all exported pages alongside the source. Changing controls invalidates the preview. Tool preview=true saves no file and displays only OCR text, never the binary. Clinical and OCR accuracy are not qualified. These controls require a configured service with document previews enabled.

Both file review and normal privacy tools use hosted NLP when configured with a hosted service. This is distinct from chat-model disclosure and does not make the operation local or offline.

docs.title: Resumable batch files
docs.text:
deidentify_batch and /privacy-batch process UTF-8 text, CSV or JSONL through the configured NLP service. Choose the source, output, checkpoint, format and selected text column/field. Batches support up to 1,000 records, 20 MB per source and 100,000 characters per selected field. The TUI requires an explicit existing FULL mode; review mode starts unchecked.

For example: “Deidentify the clinical_text column of /path/notes.csv into /path/notes.masked.csv. Use /path/notes.batch.json as the checkpoint. Mask patient and clinician identifiers, language de. I accept an unqualified draft for review.” The agent passes file paths directly to the tool. Source text and transformed text do not appear in its summary.

Only the selected field is sent to NLP. Other fields remain local and are preserved in the output; they can still contain identifiers. Each row has a status. Pending and failed selected fields are blank. Plain-text output is written only when a complete usable result exists. Review-required results remain drafts, even when every row has finished processing.

New runs require new output and checkpoint paths. Both are written atomically with owner-only permissions on macOS/Linux. The checkpoint stores opaque row IDs, offsets, counts, hashes and job cursors; source/output text, keys and policy term values are excluded. A persistent .lock file holds only a fixed marker. Keep the original input, requested output and checkpoint together for resume.

Cancel saves completed rows and requests cancellation of active service work. Resume with the same paths and controls; only rows without a saved outcome are resubmitted after cancellation, job expiry or service restart. Resume rejects changed source/output bytes, owner, deployment, model, policy or hashing-key identity. A cooperating writer lock prevents simultaneous use of one checkpoint. Recovery reconciles interruptions between output and journal writes; it is not a transaction with unrelated programs editing the same files.

The remote job holds data in process memory until deletion or expiry (15 minutes on the hosted service). The coordinator requests deletion after saving outputs; a lost connection can leave remote data until expiry. Authentication is refreshed between job requests. A timeout leaves the saved job identity available for an explicit resume. Resumable batches require a service that reports a verified deployment; there is no fallback to a non-resumable API. Using this workflow does not mean a model or language is qualified for production use.

docs.title: PHI Modes
docs.text:
OpenMed exposes three PHI modes in the TUI (/phi, or openmed agent --phi-mode at launch). Headless openmed agent --once supports full only; any other value stops with an error and sends nothing.

Mode What OpenMed enforces full No PHI-specific restrictions. Tools, workflows, and attachments work normally. deid Each typed message is first sent to the configured PII service. The model receives the text that service returns, not your original message. See the list below. strict No message is sent to a model at all.

deid and strict refuse tool calls that could return raw content to the model: PHI-gated tools, workflows that read local files, and run_workflow calls with no explicit inputs, because missing inputs would be inferred from files read earlier. No approval or allow rule can release these refusals.

In deid mode:

  • If the PII service is unavailable, or returns an incomplete or review-required result, the message is not sent and nothing is saved to the session, queue, or audit trail.
  • Attachments are rejected. Pasted text only.
  • The model can only plan, load skills, list workflows, and run workflows. Built-in web search, OPENMED.md project instructions, plan context, and raw earlier conversation history are not sent.
  • Tools that return raw content from local files or records are refused, as are MCP tools. This includes extract_pii, deidentify_text, and deidentify_batch.
  • Workflows that read local files (any file or directory input, for example note_paths) are refused, because their results quote those files. Use question-only workflows such as literature research, or work in full mode.

To work on a local file with identifiers removed, de-identify it first with /privacy (or deidentify_text) in full mode, then work from the redacted output.

Limits:

  • De-identification is automated and can miss identifiers, so identifiers it misses reach the model. It is not a regulatory de-identification determination.
  • In deid, your original text goes to the PII service first. By default that is an OpenMed-hosted service.
  • A question-only workflow can send the de-identified question to public literature and guideline sources.
  • PHI mode covers what OpenMed sends to the model. Native medical-service and MCP calls you make in full mode follow their own boundaries (see above).
  • Switching back to full removes these restrictions for later messages.

docs.title: Local Storage
docs.text:
OpenMed writes local state to files such as:

  • ~/.openmed/sessions/ for persisted TUI sessions, including conversation text and tool results. Large tool results are kept in each session's tool_results/ folder
  • ~/.openmed/history.jsonl for prompt recall. Messages typed in deid mode are not added
  • ~/.openmed/sessions/<session>/draft_snapshots/ for private, immutable workflow drafts awaiting explicit finalization. The directory is owner-only, each snapshot expires after 24 hours by default (OPENMED_DRAFT_SNAPSHOT_TTL_SECONDS), and snapshots are removed after successful finalization, session clear/rollback, or session deletion. Non-session callers use the same default policy under ~/.openmed/draft_snapshots/
  • /tmp/openmed/artifacts/ and /tmp/openmed/cases/ by default for workflow outputs. Set OPENMED_WORKFLOW_ARTIFACTS_DIR and OPENMED_WORKFLOW_CASES_DIR to keep them on managed storage
  • ~/.config/openmed/ for config, MCP metadata, profiles, and user skills
  • ~/.openmed/auth.json for OAuth credentials
  • ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json and ~/.openmed/service_secrets.json for provider and service keys you choose to store there
  • ~/.openmed/cache/ for short-lived access tokens for OpenMed-hosted services
  • ~/.openmed/batches/ and ~/.openmed/responses/ for Doubleword jobs, as described above
  • ~/.openmed/audit.json and ~/.openmed/traces/ only when optional audit traces are enabled or HF audit writes fall back locally

docs.title: Optional Audit Trail
docs.text:
Audit traces are opt-in and off by default. When enabled, they write directly from the user's machine to the configured private destination:

  • private Hugging Face Dataset repo
  • private Hugging Face Storage Bucket
  • local-only trace directory

OpenMed does not send audit traces to OpenMed-owned infrastructure. Once audit is enabled, the default audit payload mode is payload, which stores the full private transcript and tool payloads in the configured destination. Use preview, fingerprint, or none when you need a smaller or less revealing trace.

phi_payload is separate from PHI mode:

  • PHI mode describes the operator posture for the run
  • phi_payload controls what the audit trace stores

Use openmed audit status and /audit to see the active audit posture. See Audit Trail for setup and trace contents.

docs.title: Token Storage
docs.text:
openmed login writes credentials to ~/.openmed/auth.json. OpenMed ignores a project-local ./auth.json.

This is a normal local JSON file with restrictive file permissions where supported by the operating system. Teams with stricter requirements should still rely on OS-level access controls.

docs.title: Network Access
docs.text:
OpenMed can access the network for:

  • Model traffic — prompts, attachments, tool results, responses, and model catalog lookups with the configured LLM provider
  • OAuth and auth validation — browser login flow plus token validation/status checks when invoked
  • Native medical services — extraction, PII, de-identification, terminology, HCC, and RAF tooling
  • OpenMed-hosted access and assets — access tokens for hosted services, plus built-in skill instructions and workflow reference data, which are not stored in the binary
  • Public reference APIs — PubMed, MedlinePlus, and RxNorm lookups run from your machine by default
  • Web pages and search — fetch_web_page and evidence tools fetch public URLs, and search runs only if you enable web search
  • Optional audit writes — private HF dataset or bucket writes only if openmed audit enable has been configured
  • Remote MCP servers — only if you configure them
  • Release checks — openmed update and openmed --check-update contact the OpenMed release channel. The TUI also checks in the background, at most once every 24 hours. Set OPENMED_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to turn the background check off
  • Connectivity checks — commands such as openmed mcp doctor

Outside those paths, the local runtime remains local.

See Native Medical Services for the deployment patterns behind those service planes.

docs.title: No Telemetry
docs.text:
OpenMed Agent itself does not include in-product analytics, usage tracking, or background crash reporting. Public marketing and documentation pages may use lightweight site analytics to understand aggregate visitor traffic.

That statement does not cover services the agent talks to. OpenMed-hosted services see each request sent to them and keep operational records of those requests, such as the time, route, status, latency, response size, client ID, version, platform, country, a daily-salted hash of the IP address, and the user-agent product name. These records are designed to exclude request and response bodies.

Once you point OpenMed at a model provider, your own medical service, or a remote MCP server, the privacy and retention posture of that service becomes part of your real deployment boundary.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
If you need the most defensible deployment:

  1. Keep sessions and artifacts on managed local storage
  2. Treat ~/.openmed/auth.json as the single OAuth credential file and protect the user account that owns it
  3. Decide which remote boundaries may receive clinical text, and confirm that your agreements cover them. To keep native medical services off OpenMed-hosted infrastructure, run a compatible server you control
  4. Treat PHI mode as operator context, and verify the exact tool/data path for any sensitive workflow
  5. Use draft/finalize workflows so reviewers can inspect outputs before final writes

docs.title: Configuration Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles are named presets for the general CLI config file, ~/.config/openmed/config.toml. They set log_level, timeout, and use_medical_tokenizer.

Profiles do not change how the agent runs

The TUI and openmed agent --once do not read these values. Models, providers, permissions, and tools are set in runtime settings and provider configuration. Profiles are not an auth system, a model catalog, or an MCP server list.

docs.title: Built-in profiles
docs.text: Profile log_level timeout use_medical_tokenizer Intended use dev DEBUG 600 true Development and debugging prod WARNING 300 true Production-style defaults test DEBUG 60 false Tests and CI fast WARNING 120 false Faster local experiments

docs.title: Inspect and apply profiles
docs.text:
openmed config profiles
openmed config profile-show dev
openmed config profile-use prod
openmed config show --profile fast

Behavior:

  • openmed config profiles lists built-in and custom profiles
  • openmed config profile-show <name> prints the stored profile values
  • openmed config profile-use <name> merges the profile into the saved config file and records its name as profile
  • openmed config show --profile <name> previews the merged config without saving it

docs.title: Custom profiles
docs.text:
Create one from the current config:

openmed config set log_level DEBUG
openmed config set timeout 900
openmed config profile-save myprofile

Use or delete it later:

openmed config profile-use myprofile
openmed config profile-delete myprofile

Built-in profiles cannot be overwritten or deleted. profile-save copies every key from the current config except hf_token and profile.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Custom profiles are stored as TOML files under:

~/.config/openmed/profiles/<name>.toml

For example:

# OpenMed profile: myprofile
# Custom profile configuration

default_org = "OpenMed"
cache_dir = "/home/you/.cache/openmed"
device = null
log_level = "DEBUG"
timeout = 900
use_medical_tokenizer = true
medical_tokenizer_exceptions = null

docs.title: Environment variable
docs.text:
You can also set:

export OPENMED_PROFILE=prod

This only fills in the profile name when the config file has none. It does not load that profile's values; use openmed config profile-use for that.

docs.title: Resolution precedence
docs.text:
openmed config show builds its output in this order, with later steps winning:

  1. Built-in defaults
  2. Config file (~/.config/openmed/config.toml, including anything profile-use wrote)
  3. --profile <name> on openmed config show, for that one display
  4. Environment variables OPENMED_USE_MEDICAL_TOKENIZER and OPENMED_MEDICAL_TOKENIZER_EXCEPTIONS

HF_TOKEN and OPENMED_PROFILE apply only when the file leaves hf_token or profile empty. CLI flags such as --model, --agent, and --phi-mode are not part of this config. They override runtime settings for one run.

For environment variables and path details, see Configuration.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is a remote inference service. OpenMed supports OpenAI (via an API key or a ChatGPT OAuth sign-in), Anthropic, OpenRouter, Xiaomi MiMo token plans, Doubleword, and custom endpoints for the interactive agent. Doubleword also supports async Responses and 24-hour JSONL batches. The interactive agent uses the same medical tools, workflows, and audit trail across providers.

This page covers credentials, model selection, and the behaviour specific to each provider. For runtime settings that are not provider-related, see Configuration.

docs.title: Choosing a provider
docs.text:
Provider Auth Use it for OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY (recommended), or ChatGPT sign-in (experimental) The default path. GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 models. Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Claude models, with prompt caching enabled by default. OpenRouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY Models beyond the OpenAI and Anthropic lists — Gemini, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, Llama and several hundred more, on one key. MiMo MIMO_API_KEY (starts with tp) Xiaomi MiMo token-plan subscriptions, with four native models ready to select. Doubleword DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY Real-time TUI, async flex Responses, and 24-hour bulk inference. Custom optional key One or more OpenAI-compatible servers you operate — vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, or gateways.

Each provider resolves its own credentials. MiMo uses only its token-plan key and fixed endpoint; it never falls back to an OpenAI, Anthropic, or OpenRouter key.

All Doubleword modes use the same Doubleword key (from the environment or provider secrets) and the fixed https://api.doubleword.ai/v1 endpoint. See Doubleword for mode selection, interactive use, Responses jobs, and batches.

You can configure more than one at a time. Which provider handles a request is decided by the model you select — see How a provider is selected.

docs.title: Where credentials live
docs.text:
Path Holds ~/.openmed/auth.json ChatGPT OAuth tokens, written by openmed login ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json Provider API keys shared by interactive, async and batch requests, per-provider model lists, and custom endpoints ~/.openmed/settings.json Runtime behaviour such as permission mode, and your saved default model — not secrets

Store keys without hand-editing JSON:

openmed config provider-set openai --api-key "sk-..."
openmed config provider-set anthropic --api-key "sk-ant-..."
openmed config provider-set openrouter --api-key "sk-or-..."
openmed config provider-set mimo --api-key "tp-..."
openmed config provider-set doubleword --api-key "sk-..."
openmed config provider-show

provider-show reports which providers are configured without printing secret values. To remove a stored key, use --unset-api-key with the same command.

docs.title: Editing the file directly
docs.text:
provider-set writes ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json with 0600 permissions. An apiKey may be a literal string, or an {env:VAR_NAME} reference that resolves at load time — useful when the file is synced between machines and you would rather not store the secret in it:

{
  "provider": {
    "openai": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}",
        "models": ["gpt-7"]
      }
    },
    "anthropic": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}",
        "models": ["claude-opus-6"]
      }
    },
    "openrouter": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "sk-or-v1-...",
        "models": ["qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "z-ai/glm-5.2"]
      }
    },
    "mimo": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:MIMO_API_KEY}"
      }
    },
    "doubleword": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY}"
      }
    },
    "custom": {
      "options": {
        "endpoints": [
          {"baseURL": "http://localhost:8000/v1", "model": "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B", "apiKey": "{env:MY_SERVER_KEY}"}
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

Only the custom section carries endpoint URLs (inside its endpoints list) — hosted provider endpoints are fixed, and a stored baseURL on them is ignored and stripped. The gpt-7 and claude-opus-6 entries stand for IDs newer than the built-in list; see Default model and newer models.

One JSON object, one provider map

Every provider is a key inside the single provider object above. A common mistake is to paste a second example after the first, which produces two objects and makes the whole file invalid — at which point all your keys are ignored and every provider shows as not configured. If that happens, openmed config provider-show names the file and the line.

A flatter shape is accepted as an alternative to the block above — use one or the other, never both in the same file:

{
  "openrouter": {
    "api_key": "{env:OPENROUTER_API_KEY}",
    "models": ["qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "x-ai/grok-4.6"]
  }
}

Check the file is valid at any time:

openmed config provider-show

It prints which providers are configured, and exits non-zero with the parse error if the file is malformed.

Precedence is explicit runtime config → environment variable → this file → default. Provider config is read once per process, so restart OpenMed after editing the file by hand. In the TUI, opening /model also reloads it.

docs.title: Default model and newer models
docs.text:
Providers retire models and release new ones on their own schedule. OpenMed's built-in model list is a starting point, not a limit, and everything in this section works with the OpenMed you have installed.

Here, gpt-7 and claude-opus-6 stand for a newer model ID. Use the exact ID from your provider's own model page.

Use a newer model. Pass its ID directly; it does not need to be in the built-in list:

openmed --model gpt-7
openmed agent --provider anthropic --model claude-opus-6

What happens to an ID outside the built-in list depends on the provider:

  • OpenAI. IDs from the GPT-6 generation onward (gpt-6.2, gpt-7, gpt-8, and so on) route to OpenAI without being listed. OpenMed cannot know the exact reasoning range of an unlisted model, so it offers low, medium, and high: none is sent as low, and xhigh or max is sent as high. Its context window is also unknown, so automatic compaction is off for that model; use /compact in long sessions. If ChatGPT sign-in is configured too, OpenMed tries it first; use openmed agent --provider openai for your API key.
  • Older OpenAI families. GPT-5.x (except an explicit gpt-5.5), GPT-4, chatgpt-*, and o-series IDs are rejected before any request is sent, unless you add the ID to your model list below.
  • Anthropic. Any claude-* ID routes to Anthropic. An ID that contains a family OpenMed knows, such as the opus-5 in claude-opus-5-6, gets that family's thinking behaviour. Any other Claude ID runs without extended-thinking parameters, so the reasoning setting has no effect on it, and compaction assumes a conservative 200,000-token window.
  • OpenRouter and Doubleword take any model ID, from --model or your model list.
  • Custom endpoints serve whatever model each endpoint declares.
  • MiMo accepts only its four built-in IDs. Its list cannot be extended.

Add newer models to the /model picker. List them per provider. A model on your OpenAI or Anthropic list always routes to that provider, even if its ID does not match the rules above:

openmed config provider-set openai --models "gpt-7,gpt-7-mini"
openmed config provider-set anthropic --models "claude-opus-6"
# or, for one shell:
export OPENAI_MODELS="gpt-7,gpt-7-mini"
export ANTHROPIC_MODELS="claude-opus-6"

The lists are stored as models in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json:

{
  "provider": {
    "openai": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}",
        "models": ["gpt-7", "gpt-7-mini"]
      }
    },
    "anthropic": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}",
        "models": ["claude-opus-6"]
      }
    }
  }
}

An environment variable overrides the stored list for that provider. The effect of a list differs by provider:

Provider provider-set flag Environment variable Effect OpenAI --models OPENAI_MODELS Adds to the built-in models Anthropic --models ANTHROPIC_MODELS Adds to the built-in models OpenRouter --models OPENROUTER_MODELS Replaces the default list; the first entry becomes the default Doubleword --models DOUBLEWORD_MODELS Replaces the built-in list; the first entry becomes the default Custom --base-url with --model, once per endpoint OPENMED_CUSTOM_BASE_URL with OPENMED_CUSTOM_MODEL, for one endpoint Each endpoint adds one model MiMo None None The four built-in models are fixed

--unset-models removes a stored list. An ID outside the gpt- naming, or from an older OpenAI family, runs without a reasoning parameter even when listed.

Save your default model. So that you do not need --model on every launch:

openmed config model-set gpt-7 --provider openai --reasoning-effort high
openmed config model-unset    # back to the built-in default

This writes to ~/.openmed/settings.json:

{
  "model": "gpt-7",
  "provider": "openai",
  "reasoning_effort": "high"
}

provider and reasoning_effort are optional. A project's own .openmed/settings.json takes precedence over the user file. --model, --provider, and --reasoning-effort still override the saved values for a single run, and an explicit --model is never combined with a saved provider.

When a model is retired. If a provider stops serving the selected model, OpenMed says so and tells you how to pick another one, instead of showing only the raw provider error. To move on:

  1. Find the replacement ID on the provider's own model page.
  2. Try it for one run with openmed agent --model NEW_ID, adding --provider PROVIDER if the ID alone does not select the right one.
  3. Save it with openmed config model-set NEW_ID --provider PROVIDER, and add it to the picker with openmed config provider-set PROVIDER --models "NEW_ID".

A resumed session keeps the model it was saved with; switch it with /model. On OpenAI, ChatGPT sign-in, and Anthropic, background helper calls use a small built-in model (gpt-6-luna and claude-haiku-4-5). If that model is unavailable, the call is retried on your session's model, so there is nothing to configure. On every other provider, helpers use your session's model.

If a provider retires all of its built-in models, OpenMed keeps working with any ID the rules above accept. MiMo has no such route: if Xiaomi retires its models, use another provider.

Hosted provider endpoints are fixed: OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, MiMo, and Doubleword do not take a base URL through provider-set. Use the custom provider for a server or gateway you operate.

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text: The default provider. Two independent auth paths: an API key (recommended), or an experimental ChatGPT sign-in.

docs.title: API key (recommended)
docs.text:
openmed config provider-set openai --api-key "sk-..."
# or
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

Or in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json (as one key inside the single provider object — see Editing the file directly):

{
  "provider": {
    "openai": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "sk-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

No openmed login step is required when using a key. This is the supported OpenAI path.

docs.title: Sign in with ChatGPT (experimental)
docs.text:
Experimental

ChatGPT sign-in is not an officially supported OpenAI API integration. It can stop working without notice if OpenAI changes it. If sign-in or a request fails, switch to an API key: openmed config provider-set openai --api-key "sk-...", then openmed config model-set gpt-6.1-sol --provider openai (or run openmed agent --provider openai).

Uses your ChatGPT subscription rather than API billing:

openmed login             # writes ~/.openmed/auth.json
openmed oauth status
openmed oauth logout

Credentials are reused until they expire. If auth status reports the token is not valid, openmed login -f refreshes the single global auth file. openmed login --no-browser prints the authorization URL instead of opening a browser, and --timeout <seconds> extends the default five-minute wait.

An interactive sign-in can only be started by openmed login — never implicitly from inside the TUI. If you sign in from another terminal while the TUI is open, your next message picks up the new credentials without a restart.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
gpt-6.1-sol (default), gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol, and gpt-6-luna. Older OpenAI IDs such as gpt-5.6 are rejected; update a saved selection to one of these IDs. gpt-5.5 is the exception: it is not in the picker, but an explicit gpt-5.5 selection runs on the OpenAI API and needs an API key. For the picker models, OpenMed selects ChatGPT sign-in when both it and an API key are available; use --provider openai, or openmed config model-set MODEL --provider openai, to use the API key. Newer OpenAI models work too; see Default model and newer models.

GPT-6.1 Sol uses the Responses API for agent tools, has a 1,050,000-token context window, and supports low, medium (default), high, xhigh, and max reasoning. It requires reasoning: an existing none setting is mapped to low.

docs.title: Anthropic
docs.text:
openmed config provider-set anthropic --api-key "sk-ant-..."
# or
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

openmed agent --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6

Or in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json (as one key inside the single provider object — see Editing the file directly):

{
  "provider": {
    "anthropic": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "sk-ant-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Anthropic has no OAuth path — an API key is the only option. Without OpenAI credentials, a plain openmed launch uses claude-sonnet-4-6 and says so in the session. To always use another Claude model, save it as your default:

openmed config model-set claude-opus-5-5 --provider anthropic

docs.title: Models
docs.text: claude-fable-5-1, claude-opus-5-5, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-4-8, claude-sonnet-4-6 (the Anthropic default), and claude-haiku-5-5. Older IDs such as claude-opus-4-7 and claude-haiku-4-5 are not in the picker, but an explicit selection works for as long as Anthropic serves them. Selecting any claude-* model routes to Anthropic when Anthropic credentials are available, including models newer than this list (see Default model and newer models). Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 always use adaptive thinking; the other 5.x models also use adaptive thinking by default.

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
Enabled by default. OpenMed marks the stable tool schema block and the system prompt as 5-minute cache breakpoints, and enables Anthropic's top-level automatic cache control for the growing conversation, so long tool runs do not resend the entire prior transcript as fresh input every turn.

Variable Purpose Default OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_PROMPT_CACHE Enable caching for stable tool/system prefixes 1 OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL Cache TTL — 5m or 1h 5m OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_AUTOMATIC_CACHE Top-level automatic caching for multi-turn conversations 1

docs.title: Rate-limit guard
docs.text:
OpenMed also guards Claude's input-token-per-minute limits locally. Cache reads are excluded from Anthropic's rate-limit accounting, but cache writes and uncached conversation growth still count. OpenMed tracks uncached input usage, paces requests near the local budget, compacts stale history when a cache miss would make a request too large, and retries transient 429 responses using Claude's retry-after header.

Variable Purpose Default OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_RATE_LIMIT_GUARD Pace and compact before ITPM limits are exceeded 1 OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_ITPM_LIMIT Override the input-token-per-minute limit model default OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_ITPM_SAFETY_RATIO Fraction of the limit to use before pacing 0.85 OPENMED_ANTHROPIC_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES Automatic retries after a 429 2

docs.title: OpenRouter
docs.text:
OpenRouter gives you models beyond the OpenAI and Anthropic lists — Gemini, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, Llama and several hundred others — through one API key. It is a separate provider: OpenRouter credentials are never sent to OpenAI or Anthropic, and an OpenAI key is never sent to OpenRouter.

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-..."
openmed agent --provider openrouter

docs.title: Choosing which models appear
docs.text:
Configure a short list rather than all several hundred. Those models appear in their own OpenRouter group in the /model picker:

openmed config provider-set openrouter \
  --api-key "sk-or-..." \
  --models "qwen/qwen3.8-27b,z-ai/glm-5.2,minimax/minimax-m3"

Or in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json directly (as one key inside the single provider object — see Editing the file directly):

{
  "provider": {
    "openrouter": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "sk-or-v1-...",
        "models": [
          "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
          "z-ai/glm-5.2",
          "minimax/minimax-m3"
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

qwen/qwen3.8-27b is OpenMed's default OpenRouter model. The other IDs show the format; they are not recommendations.

OPENROUTER_MODELS (comma-separated) overrides the stored list for one session, and openmed config provider-set openrouter --unset-models removes it. With nothing configured, OpenMed uses qwen/qwen3.8-27b.

Browse what OpenRouter offers:

openmed config openrouter-models --search gemini
openmed config openrouter-models --all      # include models OpenMed cannot use
openmed config openrouter-models --refresh  # bypass the 24h metadata cache

docs.title: OpenRouter environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Purpose Default OPENROUTER_API_KEY The OpenRouter key. Required — OpenMed never falls back to another provider's key. unset OPENROUTER_MODELS Comma-separated model ids offered in /model; overrides the stored list stored list, else qwen/qwen3.8-27b OPENMED_OPENROUTER_MODELS_TTL_SECONDS Lifetime of cached model metadata under ~/.openmed/cache/ 86400 (24h)

The OpenRouter base URL is fixed to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1. For a self-hosted or gateway server, use the custom provider.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
OpenRouter's catalog changes often, so start from the live listing rather than a fixed list:

openmed config openrouter-models --search qwen

The listing shows only models that can drive the agent, with their capabilities. For each candidate, check:

  • Context window. OpenMed sends a large fixed tool schema on every turn, so long clinical sessions need far more than that overhead. See Context: the quiet killer.
  • Licence and terms. Open weights do not mean open for clinical use. Read the model's licence and the hosting provider's terms.
  • Data handling. Prompts reach both OpenRouter and the upstream provider that serves the model.

Check provider terms before clinical use

Terms and licences vary, and they change. Several restrict or forbid medical use; Google's Gemini API terms, for example, have prohibited use "in clinical practice, to provide medical advice". Others exclude regions, or forbid sending PHI to the provider's hosted API. Do not assume a BAA with an upstream provider covers requests routed through OpenRouter.

docs.title: Free models
docs.text:
OpenRouter serves some models on a :free tier, at no charge and with daily request limits. Use the ID exactly as the listing shows it:

openmed config openrouter-models --search :free
openmed config provider-set openrouter --api-key "sk-or-..." --models "vendor/model:free"
openmed agent --provider openrouter --model "vendor/model:free"

A long agent run makes many requests, so it reaches a daily limit much sooner than a short task, and free capacity can be less available than the paid tier of the same model. See OpenRouter's documentation for its limits. Check how a free tier handles prompts before sending anything sensitive.

docs.title: Not every OpenRouter model can run the agent
docs.text:
OpenRouter hosts image generators, audio models, and chat models without tool calling. OpenMed's tools are the product, so a model that cannot call tools cannot drive it. OpenMed reads each model's capabilities from OpenRouter's model metadata and refuses an incompatible model at startup with the reason, rather than failing part-way through a case:

OpenRouter model 'vendor/image-model' cannot drive the agent: no tool-calling
support (required by the agent). Pick a text model with tool calling — see
`openmed config openrouter-models`.

Capabilities are also enforced per request:

Capability Behavior Tool calling Required. Models without it are refused at startup. Text output Required. Image-only and audio-only models are refused. Image input Scanned documents and screenshots are sent only to vision models. On a text-only model the attachment is omitted and the message says so. Context window Taken from OpenRouter metadata, so compaction triggers at the model's real limit. Reasoning effort Clamped to the levels the model advertises, so /model never sends an effort the model rejects. Max output tokens Clamped to the model's provider cap.

The /model picker shows these as chips per model (vision · 1M ctx · reasoning), and marks a model incompatible before you select it.

docs.title: Model quality is your call
docs.text:
The compatibility check shows that a model can drive OpenMed's tools, and a high rank on a public leaderboard measures tool mechanics and reasoning. Neither measures clinical calibration: a model can run the whole tool loop smoothly and still state a confident, wrong clinical fact. It can also have weaker instruction-following, worse tool discipline, or a smaller effective context than its advertised window.

Treat an OpenRouter model as unvalidated until you have evaluated it on your own cases, and treat generated codes, doses, and clinical claims as drafts that need review, whichever model produced them. Every PHI, de-identification, and finalization gate behaves identically regardless of provider.

Prompts you send — including any PHI in them — go to OpenRouter and on to whichever upstream provider serves that model. Check OpenRouter's privacy settings for how your data is handled and whether prompt logging is enabled on your account.

docs.title: Doubleword
docs.text:
OpenMed supports three Doubleword inference modes with one key. The built-in default interactive model is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash); a configured model list uses its first entry. Choose the mode based on when you need the answer and whether requests depend on earlier results.

Mode OpenMed entry point Suitable work Real-time openmed agent --provider doubleword (streaming TUI), or openmed responses submit request.json --service-tier priority (direct CLI) Interactive questions and work where latency matters; the TUI executes agent tools Async Responses (flex) openmed responses submit request.json Background handoffs, document extraction, dependent review steps that tolerate a delay 24-hour Batch openmed batch submit requests.jsonl Independent overnight chart reviews, research screening, indexing and other backlogs

Doubleword describes flex as lower cost than real-time, and batch as lower cost than flex. background: true changes how you collect a response; it does not make a priority request cheaper. The 24-hour batch window is a completion window, not a required wait. Each dependent batch stage gets its own window. See the async, real-time, and batch service descriptions and current model pricing before choosing a tier.

docs.title: Doubleword credentials
docs.text:
export DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY="sk-your-doubleword-key"
# Or, instead of exporting the variable, store a per-user secret:
openmed config provider-set doubleword --api-key "sk-your-doubleword-key"
openmed config provider-show

Alternatively, put this entry in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json, merging it inside the existing provider object if other providers are configured:

{
  "provider": {
    "doubleword": {
      "options": {"apiKey": "sk-your-doubleword-key"}
    }
  }
}

The top-level key is provider (singular). Replace the placeholder with your key, or use "{env:DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY}" and export that variable. Keep the file private (chmod 600 ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json) and restart OpenMed after manual edits. provider-set applies those permissions automatically. An exported environment key takes precedence. All three modes use https://api.doubleword.ai/v1; no base URL or OpenAI key is needed. openmed login is unrelated.

docs.title: Try all three Doubleword modes
docs.text:
After configuring your key above, try each mode below. These examples need only the installed CLI and your key, not native medical services. Each submission uses credits; the examples use synthetic text and cap each output at 4,096 tokens, including reasoning.

1. Real-time TUI2. Async flex CLI3. 24-hour batch CLI 
openmed agent --provider doubleword --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Paste: “A synthetic document queue has six items: four reviewed and two awaiting review. Summarize that status in one sentence. No tools needed.” The answer streams in the TUI. /model lets you change models; select the Doubleword provider group.

Save this JSON object as request.json:

{
  "model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash",
  "input": "A synthetic document queue has six items: four reviewed and two awaiting review. Summarize that status in one sentence.",
  "max_output_tokens": 4096
}

openmed responses submit request.json --service-tier flex
# Replace <response-id> with the ID printed above. You can close the terminal.
openmed responses wait <response-id> --timeout 300
openmed responses results <response-id>

Submission prints a durable ID. results prints the Responses JSON object; the answer is in its output items. If waiting times out, run wait again with the same ID. To try on-demand priority through the CLI, submit a new request with --service-tier priority; polling does not make it flex-priced.

Save these two lines as requests.jsonl (one complete JSON object per line):

{"custom_id":"queue-a","method":"POST","url":"/v1/chat/completions","body":{"model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Synthetic queue A has six items, four reviewed. State how many await review."}],"max_tokens":4096}}
{"custom_id":"queue-b","method":"POST","url":"/v1/chat/completions","body":{"model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Synthetic queue B has ten items, seven reviewed. State how many await review."}],"max_tokens":4096}}

openmed batch validate requests.jsonl  # offline; no credits spent
openmed batch submit requests.jsonl
# Replace <job-id> with the ID printed above; collect later.
openmed batch wait <job-id> --timeout 300
openmed batch results <job-id> --json

results prints the paths to output.jsonl and errors.jsonl. Open those files and match each row by custom_id; successful answers are under response.body.choices[].message.content. Check errors and finish_reason too. A five-minute local timeout is normal for a batch with a 24-hour window: resume wait or results using the same ID. Never resubmit to check progress.

Use openmed responses list or openmed batch list if you lose an ID. All three examples use the same DeepSeek model. The TUI runs the interactive agent loop; openmed agent --provider doubleword --once "..." runs the same tools headlessly. See CLI workflows. Direct Responses and batch requests do not execute tools for you. The mode guide explains when to use each path, and batch inference covers overnight NLP/HCC evidence review and result handling.

docs.title: Doubleword models and picker configuration
docs.text:
With just a key, the picker offers these generation models in this order. Use the exact API IDs, including capitalization, in configuration and request bodies. The display names are not API aliases.

Display name API model ID DeepSeek V4.1 Flash deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash GLM 5.3 Flash zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash GLM 5.3 zai-org/GLM-5.3 DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 Kimi K3 moonshotai/kimi-k3 Inkling thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4 GLM 5.2 zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8 Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-NVFP4 Kimi K2.6 moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6 Nemotron 3 Super 120B A12B nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4

These are selectable defaults, not a quality ranking. Check Doubleword's catalog for availability and pricing. Shared real-time access can be rate limited.

Automatic compaction uses Doubleword's published serving windows for all 11 models: 1M for the DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi K3 and Inkling entries; 262K for Kimi K2.6 and both Nemotron entries. OpenMed carries these limits itself rather than reading them from the API, and applies the default 80% compaction threshold with space reserved for output. Any other model ID, including a dedicated alias, has an unknown window, so automatic compaction is off for it. See context and compaction for details.

Like OpenRouter, Doubleword accepts a models list under its provider options:

{
  "provider": {
    "doubleword": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY}",
        "models": [
          "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash",
          "zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash",
          "moonshotai/kimi-k3"
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

Export DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY for this example, or replace its environment reference with a literal key. Merge the entry into an existing provider object instead of replacing other providers. You can also update only the list without changing the saved key:

openmed config provider-set doubleword --models "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash,moonshotai/kimi-k3"
openmed config provider-show
openmed --models

The list replaces the built-in picker list; its first entry is the default for openmed agent --provider doubleword. Duplicates and blank entries are removed while order and ID capitalization are preserved. Dedicated aliases are accepted. Explicit --model selections still work outside the picker list. Restart after manual edits, or reopen /model to reload provider configuration.

DOUBLEWORD_MODELS (comma-separated IDs) overrides the file list. An empty or missing effective list falls back to the 11 built-ins. To restore the defaults:

unset DOUBLEWORD_MODELS
openmed config provider-set doubleword --unset-models

The list controls interactive selection only. Responses JSON and batch JSONL still require an explicit model; their request bodies are not rewritten from the picker configuration. The models list does not select an execution tier.

docs.title: Choosing the Doubleword execution mode
docs.text:
Async is selected per request, not in provider_secrets.json. Doubleword does not read an async, service_tier, or mode setting from that file, or from settings.json. The same stored key works for all modes:

What you set Where it goes API key DOUBLEWORD_API_KEY or provider.doubleword.options.apiKey in provider secrets Model, input and output-token limit The Responses JSON object or each batch JSONL row; --model for the TUI Async flex or on-demand priority openmed responses submit ... --service-tier flex (default) or --service-tier priority Bulk processing with a 24-hour completion window openmed batch submit requests.jsonl Wait in this terminal --wait on submission, or responses wait / batch wait later

For example, an overnight backlog of independent, closed-encounter reviews fits a batch: gather NLP/HCC service evidence first, then ask the model to review each record. A single report or the next step of a dependent workflow can use flex when a delay is acceptable. Interactive work belongs in the real-time TUI. See when a 24-hour batch helps.

docs.title: Doubleword real-time TUI
docs.text:
openmed agent --provider doubleword
openmed agent --provider doubleword --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
# Account-specific dedicated aliases work too:
openmed agent --provider doubleword --model yourorg-zai/GLM-5.3

Open /model and select Doubleword → DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Provider headings remain visible while searching. This is real-time streaming, including tool calls through OpenMed's existing agent loop. Helpers use Doubleword too. Selecting Doubleword in the TUI does not enable flex or batch processing. The TUI has no async mode toggle or Responses/batch job screen; use the CLI commands below for those modes. Interactive sessions use the model's default reasoning behavior; --reasoning-effort does not override it. For explicit model-supported effort settings, use reasoning.effort in a Responses request below.

Always pass --provider doubleword for an explicit model when several provider keys are configured: a namespaced model ID alone can otherwise select OpenRouter. The built-in or configured picker is a starting point; --model accepts other generation models and dedicated aliases your account can serve. Model capabilities and tier availability vary. Embedding models cannot run the interactive agent.

Doubleword describes its shared self-serve real-time endpoint as intended for development and testing, and rate limits it. Production real-time capacity is arranged separately with Doubleword; dedicated deployments use their assigned model aliases on the same API. See dedicated real-time.

docs.title: Doubleword async and on-demand CLI
docs.text:
Save this JSON object, not JSONL, as request.json:

{
  "model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash",
  "input": "Synthetic review backlog: four records have supporting evidence and two have conflicting mappings. Write a short handoff preserving the unresolved items for human review. Do not invent diagnoses or calculate risk scores.",
  "max_output_tokens": 4096
}

# Async flex: return local and remote IDs once Doubleword accepts the request.
openmed responses submit request.json --service-tier flex

# Read status or resume from another terminal, even after restarting OpenMed.
openmed responses list
openmed responses status <response-id>
openmed responses wait <response-id> --timeout 300
openmed responses results <response-id>

# On-demand priority: same lifecycle, different price/latency tier.
openmed responses submit request.json --service-tier priority --wait --timeout 120

Replace <response-id> with the local or remote ID printed by submit or list. Omitting --service-tier selects flex.

What happens after submission:

  1. OpenMed saves the request locally and sends one POST /v1/responses to Doubleword with service_tier: "flex", background: true, and stream: false.
  2. Doubleword returns a remote response ID and processes the work on its servers. You can close the terminal after submission; no local worker needs to stay up.
  3. status, wait, and results retrieve that response with GET /v1/responses/{id}. They reuse the saved ID and do not create another paid inference request.
  4. When complete, results prints the output. It stays pending while the remote work is unfinished; failures and incomplete responses must be handled separately.

Flex is a scheduling and pricing tier. background: true lets a request return an ID while work continues. This CLI also uses background polling for priority requests, which still receive priority scheduling and pricing. Async flex uses /v1/responses; bulk batches use the separate /v1/files and /v1/batches lifecycle. Flex has no 24-hour completion window, and any scheduling target Doubleword publishes is not a completion guarantee. See Doubleword's async contract.

--wait controls local polling, not provider scheduling or price. --poll-interval defaults to five seconds and must be at least one second. Omit --timeout to keep polling; a timeout applies to the polling loop and can overrun by one HTTP request.

Use --json for machine-readable status. results always prints the complete Responses object, including output items, tool calls, usage, errors and incomplete_details. A terminal incomplete response is not a successful answer, even if it contains partial text. Exit codes are 0 for success/status, 1 for terminal failure or incomplete results, 2 for errors, 3 for a local wait timeout, and 130 for interruption.

Closing the terminal or pressing Ctrl-C does not cancel remote work. Resume the saved ID; do not submit the same request again to check progress. If a creation request loses its connection, the local state is submission_unknown (or submitting after a hard interruption). Inspect Doubleword's Responses dashboard and attach the existing remote ID with:

openmed responses adopt <remote-response-id>
openmed responses wait <remote-response-id>

There is no Responses cancellation command. Batch cancellation is available through openmed batch cancel. An HTTP 402/403/429 indicates a credits, access, or rate-limit issue; automatic paid retries are disabled.

docs.title: Doubleword structured input and dependent steps
docs.text:
Responses request JSON passes through instructions, message-array input, previous_response_id, tools, tool_choice, text.format, reasoning, and other provider-supported fields. submit requires a positive integer max_output_tokens, and rejects stream: true, background: false, and store: false. The default model may consume part of the output budget for reasoning. Use only the reasoning levels your model supports.

Direct Responses and Batch commands do not execute OpenMed tools. If output contains a function_call, your orchestrator must execute the tool, then submit its result in the next request. A completed inference response is not evidence that the whole workflow finished. For automatic interactive tool execution, use the TUI, or headless --once for scripts. For overnight NLP/HCC work, prepare independent service evidence first, then submit one batch of model reviews; see the retrospective backlog example.

Model-supported image input, structured output and tool definitions can be included in request JSON. OpenMed has no direct embeddings command: use an embedding model through embedding batches, or call Doubleword's embeddings API from your own client.

docs.title: Doubleword storage and data boundary
docs.text:
Individual Responses snapshots, submitted request bodies and collected output are stored with owner-only permissions under ~/.openmed/responses/. Override with OPENMED_RESPONSES_DIR or relocate the whole home with OPENMED_HOME. status --no-refresh, results --no-refresh, and list work offline. Batch files remain under ~/.openmed/batches/; TUI sessions use normal session storage. Credentials are not written into job snapshots.

These are hosted inference calls. Direct JSON/JSONL input is sent as supplied and is not transformed by the TUI's PHI setting. Review your inputs and the provider's storage policies before submitting sensitive material. Background Responses retain state remotely for retrieval; store:false is rejected by the resumable CLI. Local deletion does not delete provider-side data.

docs.title: Xiaomi MiMo token plan
docs.text:
For a Xiaomi MiMo token-plan subscription, store your key once. The commands below use a placeholder; replace it with your own tp key:

openmed config provider-set mimo --api-key "tp-..."
openmed agent --provider mimo

Or export the key for the current shell:

export MIMO_API_KEY="tp-..."
openmed agent --provider mimo

Neither method requires openmed login. An exported MIMO_API_KEY takes precedence over the stored key. If MiMo is your only configured provider, openmed also selects the default MiMo model.

Only the API key is required. All four models are preconfigured in Ctrl+M / /model:

  • mimo-v2.5-pro — default; text input.
  • mimo-v2.5 — text and image input.
  • mimo-v2.6-pro — text and image input.
  • mimo-v2.6-flash — text input.

Select a model at launch with:

openmed agent --provider mimo --model mimo-v2.6-pro
openmed agent --provider mimo --model mimo-v2.6-flash

Keys starting with tp use https://token-plan-ams.xiaomimimo.com/v1. This provider supports token-plan subscriptions only. Pay-as-you-go keys starting with sk are rejected with an explanatory message; they are never sent to the token-plan endpoint. No base URL or model list needs to be configured.

docs.title: MiMo provider secrets example
docs.text:
For a MiMo-only setup, the complete ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json file is:

{
  "provider": {
    "mimo": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "tp-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Replace tp-... with your token-plan key. If the file already contains other providers, add only the mimo entry inside its existing provider object; keep the other entries. The combined example shows all providers together. Do not add a second top-level JSON object.

To keep the actual key in the environment, use this alternative complete file:

{
  "provider": {
    "mimo": {
      "options": {
        "apiKey": "{env:MIMO_API_KEY}"
      }
    }
  }
}

Export MIMO_API_KEY before launching OpenMed. A reference resolves only when that variable is set in the OpenMed process. When editing the file manually, keep its permissions private (chmod 600 ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json) and restart OpenMed to reload it. provider-set applies those permissions automatically. Keys belong in this per-user file or the environment, never in project settings or a repository.

docs.title: MiMo configuration reference
docs.text: Setting Behavior Provider ID mimo Environment variable MIMO_API_KEY; overrides the stored key Stored key provider.mimo.options.apiKey Key type Starts with tp; sk pay-as-you-go keys are unsupported Base URL https://token-plan-ams.xiaomimimo.com/v1; selected automatically Default model mimo-v2.5-pro Built-in models mimo-v2.5-pro, mimo-v2.5, mimo-v2.6-pro, mimo-v2.6-flash Model list Built in and fixed; --models is not accepted Context window 1M for the V2.5 models. Unknown for the V2.6 models, so automatic compaction is off for them; use /compact in long sessions Transport Streaming OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions Inference boundary Hosted by Xiaomi; the token plan is not local or offline inference

docs.title: Thinking and attachments
docs.text:
Thinking is enabled by default. Choose Thinking off in the reasoning picker, or pass --reasoning-effort none, to disable it. Other effort values enable thinking without selecting a strength. OpenMed preserves the provider's returned reasoning_content across tool calls and follow-up turns as required by MiMo's conversation protocol. Workflow helper calls use the same token-plan key and selected model, with thinking disabled for their short outputs. OpenMed forwards images to mimo-v2.5 and mimo-v2.6-pro. Images attached with the other MiMo models are omitted with a notice.

openmed agent --provider mimo --reasoning-effort none  # thinking off
openmed agent --provider mimo --reasoning-effort medium  # thinking on

docs.title: Startup latency and TUI status
docs.text:
The direct token-plan route and OpenRouter's namespaced MiMo route are separate services. They use different credentials, endpoints, and serving infrastructure, so their time to first output can differ substantially even for the same model family. Fast generation after output begins does not imply a fast first token.

The TUI distinguishes the stages:

Status Meaning Preparing request… OpenMed is applying request/privacy routing and may run a short same-provider workflow-intent helper call. The primary model stream has not started yet. Waiting for model response… The primary request has been dispatched, but OpenMed has not received a non-empty reasoning or answer delta. Model is reasoning… The provider has emitted reasoning_content; OpenMed is rendering it live.

Choosing --reasoning-effort none disables MiMo's generated thinking, but it does not control provider queueing, connection setup, or time to first output. If Preparing request… is slow, the delay is before the primary stream. If Waiting for model response… is slow, the request has reached the provider path and OpenMed is waiting for model output. OpenMed forwards the first non-empty reasoning_content or answer delta to the TUI as soon as it arrives.

docs.title: Verify, replace, or remove the key
docs.text:
openmed config provider-show
openmed --models
openmed config provider-set mimo --api-key "tp-..."  # replace the stored key
openmed config provider-set mimo --unset-api-key    # remove the stored key

provider-show reports set without printing the key. After removing a stored key, an exported MIMO_API_KEY still takes precedence; use unset MIMO_API_KEY to remove it from the current shell too.

Symptom What to check MiMo asks for a key Set MIMO_API_KEY or store provider.mimo.options.apiKey; check provider-show for malformed JSON or an unresolved environment reference. Pay-as-you-go key rejected Use the tp key from your token-plan subscription. sk keys are not supported by this provider. Unsupported model Use mimo-v2.5-pro, mimo-v2.5, mimo-v2.6-pro, or mimo-v2.6-flash. Namespaced xiaomi/... IDs belong to the separate OpenRouter route. Slow before reasoning appears Check the current TUI status. Preparing request… is pre-stream work; Waiting for model response… means the primary request was dispatched but the provider has not emitted model output. Compare the direct token-plan route with OpenRouter only as separate serving paths. --base-url or --models rejected MiMo's endpoint and model list are built in. Configure only the key, then select a model with --model at launch. Replacing the stored key has no effect Check whether MIMO_API_KEY is still exported, then restart OpenMed.

docs.title: Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints
docs.text:
The custom provider points OpenMed at servers you operate — vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, or a company gateway. Serving engines launch one model per endpoint, so the configuration is a list of endpoints, each with its own base URL, optional credential, and the one model it serves. Selecting a model routes the session to the endpoint that declares it. The hosted providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, MiMo, Doubleword) deliberately have no base-URL configuration — a provider means one thing, and any stored base URL for them is ignored and stripped.

Add one endpoint per model:

openmed config provider-set custom --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 --model "nvidia/Nemotron-3-Super-120B"
openmed config provider-set custom --base-url https://gpu2.example.org/v1 --model "Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B" --api-key sk-host2
openmed config provider-set custom --base-url http://192.168.1.40:8000/v1 --model "poolside/Laguna"

openmed config endpoint-doctor http://localhost:8000/v1   # validate each FIRST
openmed agent --provider custom --model "poolside/Laguna"

--base-url and --model go together, because one endpoint serves one model. Re-running with the same --model updates that endpoint (a stored key is kept unless you pass a new one); --remove-model <id> deletes it. With no --model, openmed agent --provider custom uses the first endpoint. A plain openmed launch uses it when no other provider is configured; to use a specific model every time, save it with openmed config model-set "poolside/Laguna" --provider custom.

Or in ~/.openmed/provider_secrets.json directly — an endpoints list under the custom section:

{
  "provider": {
    "custom": {
      "options": {
        "endpoints": [
          {"baseURL": "http://localhost:8000/v1", "model": "nvidia/Nemotron-3-Super-120B"},
          {"baseURL": "https://gpu2.example.org/v1", "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B", "apiKey": "{env:HOST2_KEY}"},
          {"baseURL": "http://192.168.1.40:8000/v1", "model": "poolside/Laguna"}
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

apiKey is optional per endpoint (local servers are commonly keyless) and supports literal or {env:VAR} forms. The same one-object-one-provider-map rule from Editing the file directly applies.

For a quick test without touching the file, environment variables declare one additional endpoint: OPENMED_CUSTOM_BASE_URL, OPENMED_CUSTOM_MODEL, and optionally OPENMED_CUSTOM_API_KEY. They win over a stored endpoint that declares the same model.

What the provider does for you at startup:

  • Routes by model. Each session talks only to the endpoint declaring its model, with that endpoint's own credential — keys never cross hosts, and your OPENAI_API_KEY can never silently travel to your own server.
  • Consults the endpoint's /models listing. A model the server does not actually serve fails immediately, naming what it does serve.
  • Reads the served context window (vLLM/SGLang max_model_len) for automatic compaction. A server that reports none pins the window to unknown — automatic compaction is off for that session (see Context And Compaction) and a hosted catalog namesake can never supply a fabricated number.
  • Sends the safe request shape. Chat Completions only, temperature omitted, streamed usage requested, and the runtime guard refuses a turn whose "text" is really an unparsed tool call.
  • Refuses cleartext keys to remote hosts — plain http:// with a stored key is allowed only for localhost and private networks, enforced both in the CLI and again at resolution so a hand-edited file cannot bypass it.

Configured models appear as a Custom endpoint group in the /model picker, each row naming the host that serves it.

What custom models are not

OpenMed cannot vouch for the model you serve. Tool-calling discipline, clinical quality and safety behaviour are yours to validate — endpoint-doctor proves the plumbing, not the medicine. Check your engine's documentation for the exact --tool-call-parser value: a wrong one fails silently.

docs.title: Checking an endpoint before you trust it
docs.text:
openmed config endpoint-doctor tells you whether an OpenAI-compatible server — your own vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or Ollama, or a gateway — can actually drive the agent. It changes nothing in your configuration. It does send a few real chat requests, including one the size of a full OpenMed turn, so a metered endpoint may bill them.

openmed config endpoint-doctor http://localhost:8000/v1

A healthy endpoint:

Endpoint: http://localhost:8000/v1
Model:    openmed-local

  [PASS] reachable: Connected to http://localhost:8000/v1.
  [PASS] auth: Credentials accepted.
  [PASS] models: 1 model(s) served: openmed-local
  [PASS] context: Context window 65,536 tokens.
  [PASS] streaming: Server streamed a response (SSE).
  [PASS] tools: Model emitted a streamed tool call.
  [PASS] tool_call_index: Tool-call deltas carry `index`.
  [PASS] temperature: Model accepts `temperature`.
  [PASS] truncation: Front of the prompt survived — no silent truncation.

Result: usable by OpenMed (2.4s)

Exit codes are 0 usable, 1 not usable, 2 bad input — so it works in CI. An endpoint is usable when nothing failed and the reachable, models, context, streaming and tools checks all ran; a warning does not block it.

Flag Purpose Default --model Model to test First model the endpoint serves --api-key Key for the endpoint. Prefer OPENMED_ENDPOINT_API_KEY OPENMED_ENDPOINT_API_KEY, then OPENROUTER_API_KEY for an OpenRouter URL --quick Send one tool instead of OpenMed's full tool schema. Faster, but it will not surface large-tool-array failures Off --timeout Per-request timeout in seconds 30 --json Emit the same report as JSON Off

The doctor does not read keys stored with provider-set. For an endpoint that needs a key, set OPENMED_ENDPOINT_API_KEY before running it.

docs.title: What it checks, and why
docs.text: Check Catches reachable Wrong port, wrong scheme, DNS typo, TLS mismatch — each reported distinctly auth Missing or wrong API key (self-hosted servers 401; public catalogs do not) models Server up but serving nothing, or a listing that is not OpenAI-shaped model A --model the server does not serve context A window too small for OpenMed's fixed per-turn overhead, or a server that reports no window streaming Gateways that buffer and break SSE — OpenMed only streams tools Tool calling disabled, unsupported, or rejected with OpenMed's full tool array leaked_tool_call The safety check — a wrong tool-call parser returning tool syntax as prose leaked_reasoning A warning: reasoning markers such as </think> in the answer, because no reasoning parser is configured tool_call_index Streamed deltas missing index, which breaks parallel calls finish_reason Shapes the runtime rejects, which would crash on the first tool turn temperature A warning: reasoning models that reject the parameter, which OpenMed then omits truncation Servers that silently drop the front of a long prompt, where the system prompt and tool schemas sit

docs.title: The failure that matters most
docs.text:
If the server's tool-call parser is missing or wrong, it returns the tool call as plain text with tool_calls empty and finish_reason: "stop". There is no error, and in a clinical agent that text is indistinguishable from real content. The doctor fails the endpoint and names the fix:

  [FAIL] leaked_tool_call: The model returned tool syntax as PLAIN TEXT
         (XML <tool_call> (Qwen 3.5+, GLM, MiniMax)) with no tool_calls
         (finish_reason='stop'). The server is not parsing tool calls.
          -> The tool-call parser is missing or wrong. vLLM needs BOTH
          -> --enable-auto-tool-choice AND --tool-call-parser <name> (there is no
          -> 'auto'); SGLang needs --tool-call-parser. Use the value for this model
          -> family — e.g. Qwen 3.5+ is `qwen3_coder`, NOT `hermes`; GLM is `glm47`;
          -> Gemma 4 is `gemma4`; MiniMax is `minimax_m3` on vLLM but `minimax-m3` on
          -> SGLang. See the providers guide:
          -> https://agent.openmed.life/docs/providers/

It also catches the harder version of this, where a parser matches the first tool call and leaks the rest as text — the case that otherwise looks healthy.

docs.title: Context: the quiet killer
docs.text:
OpenMed sends about 95 tool schemas (about 23,000 tokens) plus its system prompt on every turn. A window below that truncates every request:

  [FAIL] context: Context window is 16,384 tokens; OpenMed's tool schema alone
         is 23,167. Every request would be truncated.
          -> Raise the served context to at least 65,536: vLLM --max-model-len 65536,
          -> SGLang --context-length 65536, llama.cpp --ctx-size 65536 (its default is
          -> 4096), Ollama OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536 before `ollama serve` (its
          -> default auto-scales and can land at 4k — verify with `ollama ps`).

The check fails below about 43,000 tokens (the tool schema plus 20,000 tokens of working room), warns below 65,536, and passes at 65,536 or above.

It also fails when the server reports no window at all. vLLM and SGLang report one on /v1/models; llama.cpp and Ollama may not. OpenMed can still run such a server, with automatic compaction off and a one-time notice in the TUI, but only the server's own settings protect you from truncation, so confirm its served context yourself.

docs.title: Serving your own model
docs.text:
Each model family needs its own launch flags, including the exact --tool-call-parser value:

Model family --tool-call-parser Qwen 3.5 and later qwen3_coder, not hermes GLM glm47 Gemma 4 gemma4 MiniMax minimax_m3 on vLLM, minimax-m3 on SGLang

Parser names belong to the serving engine and can change between engine versions, so check its documentation too. For example, to serve Qwen 3.8 27B on one GPU:

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B \
  --served-model-name openmed-local \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --max-model-len 65536 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --api-key sk-openmed-CHANGEME

export OPENMED_ENDPOINT_API_KEY=sk-openmed-CHANGEME
openmed config endpoint-doctor http://localhost:8000/v1

openmed config provider-set custom --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \
  --model openmed-local --api-key sk-openmed-CHANGEME
openmed agent --provider custom

Credentials

Prefer OPENMED_ENDPOINT_API_KEY over --api-key: arguments are visible in ps and shell history. The doctor refuses to send a key over cleartext http:// to a non-local host, strips any user:pass@ from the URL before printing anything, and never echoes the key into its output.

docs.title: Web search
docs.text: Web search is off by default on every provider, including OpenAI and ChatGPT OAuth. When enabled it runs client-side, so it behaves identically on Anthropic, OpenRouter, MiMo, Doubleword, or a local model. Enabling it sends search queries to a third-party vendor, so it is an explicit operator decision. See Web Search.

docs.title: How a provider is selected
docs.text:
The TUI defaults to gpt-6.1-sol with medium reasoning. When multiple providers are configured, the model you select determines the provider:

  • A model declared on a custom endpoint always uses that endpoint.
  • claude-* models use Anthropic when Anthropic credentials are available.
  • GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 models use ChatGPT OAuth first when ~/.openmed/auth.json exists, then fall back to the OpenAI key. Explicit GPT-5.5 selections prefer an API key when available.
  • Bare mimo-v2.5-pro, mimo-v2.5, mimo-v2.6-pro, and mimo-v2.6-flash IDs use MiMo token-plan credentials.
  • Namespaced model ids (vendor/model, such as qwen/qwen3.8-27b) use OpenRouter when its key is configured. Without an OpenRouter key, a configured Doubleword key can select Doubleword for these IDs. Use --provider doubleword explicitly to select Doubleword when both keys are present.
  • Selecting the Doubleword group in /model, or passing --provider doubleword, selects its real-time adapter. Its default model is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; async and batch jobs use their own CLI commands.

An ordinary launch with no --model starts from gpt-6.1-sol, which needs an OpenAI key or ChatGPT sign-in. If the selected model belongs to a provider you have no credentials for, OpenMed switches to another configured provider's default model and says so in the session, in this order:

  1. Anthropic: claude-sonnet-4-6
  2. ChatGPT sign-in or an OpenAI key: gpt-6.1-sol
  3. OpenRouter: your OpenRouter default model
  4. MiMo: mimo-v2.5-pro
  5. Doubleword: the Doubleword default model
  6. A custom endpoint: the first configured model

With no credentials at all, the TUI says what to configure and waits. Your next message picks up credentials added from another terminal. --once never replaces a model you named and exits with an error instead.

Choose the model at launch, or at runtime with Ctrl+M or /model:

openmed agent --model gpt-6.1-sol --reasoning-effort medium
openmed agent --provider openrouter --model qwen/qwen3.8-27b
openmed agent --provider doubleword --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

--provider forces a specific provider; omit it to let the model decide.

docs.title: Reasoning effort
docs.text:
The picker exposes model-specific values. GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra offer low, medium, high, xhigh, and max; GPT-6 Sol and Luna also offer none. GPT-5.5 stops at xhigh. OpenAI models outside the built-in list offer low, medium, and high. Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and Haiku 5.5 offer low, medium, high, xhigh, and max; Sonnet 4.6 offers low, medium, high, and max. extra_high is accepted as a compatibility alias: it resolves to xhigh on OpenAI models and max on Claude models.

MiMo treats none as thinking off and any other value as thinking on. Doubleword interactive sessions ignore the setting and use the model's default. openmed --models explains each mode.

For OpenRouter models the effort is clamped to the levels that model actually advertises, so a selection is never rejected by the provider.

Provider keys vs native medical services

OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, MiMo, and Doubleword keys are model-provider credentials. OpenMed's native medical services — extraction, PII, de-identification, terminology, coding — are a separate service plane with their own configuration. See Native Medical Services.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills are markdown instruction overlays that change how the agent approaches a task. They are not the same thing as agent modes, and they are not a mechanism for registering new native medical backends.

OpenMed ships 21 built-in skills. You can also add your own local skills.

Built-in skills are delivered by an OpenMed-hosted service, not stored in the binary. If that service is unreachable, they report that they are temporarily unavailable; see When a service is unavailable. Your own skills load from your machine.

docs.title: What skills do
docs.text:
Skills can:

  • add domain-specific instructions
  • bias the workflow shape the model follows
  • provide reusable task framing for common jobs
  • optionally carry metadata such as allowed_tools

Important boundary:

  • skills are prompt/instruction overlays
  • allowed_tools is descriptive metadata and does not restrict tools. Tool limits come from agent mode, access mode, runtime settings, PHI mode, and file privacy

docs.title: How to use skills
docs.text:
Use any of these entry points:

  • type $ in the TUI to browse skills
  • run /skill in the TUI
  • launch with openmed agent --skill <skill-id>
  • ask the agent to load a specific skill

Example:

openmed agent --skill reviewing-prior-auth

docs.title: Built-in skills
docs.text:
Skill ID Purpose analyzing-clinical-text Clinical entity extraction, note comparison, medication review, and related text analysis analyzing-experimental-data Method for deriving results from assay, omics, dose-response, plate, or imaging data. Its steps call for code-execution tools that are not in the default tool set analyzing-health-data Multi-source consumer record import, trend analysis, reconciliation, visit prep, narratives, and optional FHIR-oriented output authoring-openmed-skills OpenMed skill creation rules and workflow routing auditing-medical-codes ICD-10 specificity review, terminology cross-checks, coding compliance, and HCC / RAF-oriented audits care-coordination Inbox triage, discharge handoff, adapter-prepared input packs, follow-up tasks, and reviewer-safe patient drafts citing-evidence Source registry, inline citation ID, PubMed, official guidance, deep-research outputs, and evidence-gap rules developing-fhir FHIR R4 implementation, validation, and debugging documenting-clinical-visits SOAP-note generation from visit transcripts with coding hints drafting-trial-protocols Structured trial protocol drafting from provided inputs escalating-to-reviewer Reviewer-gated draft/finalize behavior with approval tokens and reviewer metadata explaining-eob-claims Plain-language explanation of EOB and claim data handling-phi-disclosure Output-side PHI disclosure, redaction, local artifact safety, and audit notes managing-case-context Explicit case-scoped context using case_id and local case workspaces preparing-clinical-artifacts Clinical artifact packaging across PDF, DOCX, XLSX, Markdown, and JSON processing-pii PII detection, extraction, and de-identification workflows researching-literature PubMed search, abstract retrieval, clinical literature deep research, and evidence synthesis reviewing-appeals Appeal review against denial requirements and evidence gaps reviewing-prior-auth Prior-auth review against codes and LCD/NCD criteria running-clinical-workflows Guidance for deterministic workflows plus domain, evidence, PHI, reviewer, case-context, and artifact skill pairing special-pathogen-triage Returned-traveler fever/VHF workups with official-source evidence and reviewer-gated packets

Two practical rules:
