  • pair analyzing-health-data with --agent consumer when you want the restricted personal-health lane
  • pair care-coordination with --agent coordination when you want inbox/discharge work plus reviewer-safe finalize flows

docs.title: Workflow skill recommendations
docs.text:
Deterministic workflows expose skill guidance in two places:

  • list_workflows() returns recommended_skills for each workflow.
  • Successful run_workflow(...) results include recommended_skills plus a short skill_hint.

This matters when an agent jumps straight to a workflow. The workflow still runs deterministically, but the skill recommendations tell the model which overlays to load before summarizing the receipt, writing artifact commentary, or finalizing reviewer-gated output.

Common pairings:

Workflow Recommended skills clinical_literature_research researching-literature, citing-evidence, preparing-clinical-artifacts special_pathogen_workup special-pathogen-triage, citing-evidence, escalating-to-reviewer, handling-phi-disclosure, preparing-clinical-artifacts prior_auth_review / appeal_review Domain review skill, citing-evidence, escalating-to-reviewer, handling-phi-disclosure, preparing-clinical-artifacts clinical_inbox_triage / discharge_handoff care-coordination, escalating-to-reviewer, handling-phi-disclosure, preparing-clinical-artifacts, managing-case-context

Domain skills also include Companion skills sections so the graph works in the other direction: if the agent starts by loading reviewing-prior-auth, the skill points it toward the reusable evidence, reviewer, PHI, and artifact guardrails.

docs.title: Add your own skills
docs.text:
Custom skills load from:

  • ~/.config/openmed/skills/
  • or OPENMED_SKILLS_DIR if you override the directory

Supported formats:

  • a flat markdown file named <skill-id>.md
  • a package directory named <skill-id>/SKILL.md

The filename or folder name becomes the skill ID used by $, /skill, load_skill, and openmed agent --skill. A skill ID is a single name: load_skill refuses path-like names, so it cannot read a file by path.

docs.title: Example: flat markdown skill
docs.text:
~/.config/openmed/skills/payer-policy-review.md

---
description: Review payer policy context before prior auth analysis.
allowed_tools:
  - search_pubmed
  - mcp__guidelines__*
---

Always check the payer policy toolset before drafting the recommendation.
Prefer policy citations over generic summaries when both are available.

docs.title: Example: package skill
docs.text:
~/.config/openmed/skills/payer-policy-review/SKILL.md

Review payer policy context before prior auth analysis.

Always check the payer policy toolset before drafting the recommendation.
Prefer policy citations over generic summaries when both are available.

docs.title: Skill loading behavior
docs.text:
• New or edited skills are picked up on restart
  • User skills can override built-in skills by reusing the same skill ID
  • The TUI skill picker shows built-in and user skills together
  • User-added skills and user-added MCP servers are supported
  • New native medical tools cannot be added; use MCP for external tools
  • DOCX, XLSX, and case-context work are native tools; the matching skills only guide when and how to use them

docs.title: Skill vs agent mode vs MCP
docs.text:
Use the right surface for the right job:

Surface Use it when... Skill You want reusable instructions for how the agent should approach a task Agent mode You want a different tool-access boundary: clinical, consumer, or coordination MCP You need external tools or data sources that are not already part of OpenMed's native tool inventory

docs.title: Example prompts
docs.text:
Load the reviewing-prior-auth skill and review this request against LCD criteria.

Load the documenting-clinical-visits skill and turn this transcript into a structured SOAP note.

Load the running-clinical-workflows skill and run a chart summary on /path/intake_note.txt

Load the analyzing-health-data skill, import this FHIR export, and run a draft consumer_summary with timeline, trends, reconciliation notes, and visit-prep questions.

Load the care-coordination skill, normalize this portal export into a thread pack, and run a draft clinical_inbox_triage workflow.

docs.title: Agent TUI
docs.text: OpenMed's TUI is the main operator interface: a terminal chat surface with visible plans, tool calls, structured workflow cards, local session persistence, and model/skill switching.

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
openmed
openmed --model gpt-6.1-sol
openmed --models
openmed agent --model gpt-6.1-sol --reasoning-effort medium

docs.title: What the interface shows
docs.text:
A normal run can include:

  • your prompt and attached files
  • a visible plan
  • inline tool calls and results
  • model text and optional reasoning summary
  • workflow cards and artifact references

The key idea is that work stays inspectable in the conversation instead of disappearing behind a background job.

docs.title: Input model
docs.text:
The input box reacts to these prefixes:

Prefix or action What it does plain text Normal chat request @ Attach file paths inline # MCP autocomplete $ Skill autocomplete / Slash-command autocomplete

Useful behaviors:

  • Enter sends a message
  • Shift+Enter or Ctrl+J inserts a newline
  • Up and Down browse input history
  • Enter while a run is active steers the current run
  • Tab while a run is active queues a follow-up to send after the current run finishes
  • Tab or Enter accepts the highlighted autocomplete entry
  • drag/drop files or folders pastes absolute paths

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Key Action Ctrl+Q Quit Ctrl+C or Esc Interrupt the current run. When idle, these close an open dialog or autocomplete list, then clear the input Ctrl+L Clear the conversation and its context Ctrl+P Open the command palette Ctrl+O Switch or create a session Ctrl+M Open the model picker Shift+Tab Cycle agent mode F1 Open help

Many terminals send Ctrl+M as Enter, so it can submit the input instead of opening the picker. /model works in every terminal. Likewise, Ctrl+J inserts a newline where Shift+Enter is not reported.

docs.title: Model picker
docs.text:
The model picker is a three-step flow:

  1. Choose a model
  2. Choose a model-specific reasoning effort
  3. On supported models, choose whether to show reasoning summaries

You can open it with /model or Ctrl+M.

Doubleword is available once its key is configured. Select Doubleword → DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for real-time streaming and the usual agent tools, or launch with openmed agent --provider doubleword. Provider headings stay visible in search results. Async Responses and 24-hour batches are managed in another terminal using openmed responses and openmed batch; they do not have TUI job screens. See Doubleword for mode selection. The Doubleword group offers 11 built-in models. Set models in its provider options, or use openmed config provider-set doubleword --models "id1,id2", to replace the list; the first entry is its launch default. Reopening /model reloads the configuration. Use exact IDs from the Doubleword model table.

The first step opens with a search box focused, so you can just start typing: the list filters live on model id, display name, or provider, keeping provider headings visible while you search. For example, MiMo token-plan models stay under MiMo, separate from MiMo models served through OpenRouter. Without a query, models are grouped into sections — Favorites, Recent, then one section per configured provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, MiMo, Doubleword, OpenRouter, Custom endpoint). Each row shows the model on the left and its source or capabilities dimmed on the right; the current model carries a ● marker and favorites a ★.

Key Action type Filter the list as you type ↑ / ↓ Move the highlight, even while the search box has focus Enter Select the highlighted model Ctrl+F Star or unstar the highlighted model (persisted in ~/.openmed/settings.json) Esc Close without changing the model

Selecting a model records it under Recent. A favorited or recent model is listed once, in that section, rather than repeated in its provider section. If the same model id is configured under two providers (a model served on a local endpoint that also exists on OpenRouter), each appears under its own provider and selecting one routes to exactly that provider.

GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra expose low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Sol and Luna also expose none, which skips the reasoning-summary step. The default GPT-6.1 Sol session applies medium reasoning with thinking display off. An existing none setting maps to low on models that require reasoning.

With a MiMo token-plan key configured, the MiMo section includes mimo-v2.5-pro (default, text), mimo-v2.5 (text and images), mimo-v2.6-pro (text and images), and mimo-v2.6-flash (text). The reasoning picker offers Thinking on and Thinking off. Choosing off sends thinking.type=disabled; other effort values enable thinking. No model-list configuration is required. See MiMo setup for the key-only setup and provider_secrets.json examples.

During a turn, the activity label identifies where startup time is being spent:

Status Meaning Preparing request… Request/privacy routing is running; a same-provider helper call may also run before the primary model request. Waiting for model response… The primary request has been sent, but no reasoning or answer delta has arrived. Model is reasoning… Provider-returned reasoning is streaming into the visible reasoning block.

This distinction is especially useful with MiMo token plans: the direct Xiaomi route and a namespaced xiaomi/... model on OpenRouter are different serving paths and can have very different time to first output. See MiMo startup latency and TUI status.

docs.title: Agent modes
docs.text:
The TUI can switch among three agent modes:

Mode Behavior clinical Full registered tool access consumer Restricted safety-first allowlist for personal health workflows coordination Restricted care-coordination lane for inbox triage, discharge handoff, and reviewer-safe patient drafts

You can switch modes with Shift+Tab or /agent.

The same three modes are available from the CLI with openmed agent --agent ....

docs.title: Access modes
docs.text:
Access modes set how tools are gated, separately from the agent mode. Switch with /access. The choice is saved with the session, and new sessions start in Ask.

Mode Permission mode Behavior Ask auto Approval-gated tools prompt; see Permission policy Read-only plan Only read-only tools run, for exploring and planning Full access acceptall Tools run without per-call approval unless denied

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Sessions persist locally and keep:

  • conversation history
  • model and reasoning settings
  • active skill
  • agent mode and access mode
  • PHI mode
  • plan history
  • durable global plan paths for long runs
  • tool and card output

Use Ctrl+O or /session to switch sessions or create a new one. To resume one at launch, pass openmed --session <id>.

docs.title: Long sessions
docs.text:
The TUI is built to keep a single session running for hours without getting heavy:

  • Scroll-up history. Opening a session mounts only the newest messages; older ones stream in automatically as you scroll toward the top — there is no "load more" button to click. During a live run the oldest rows are likewise pruned back into that scroll-up history so the widget count stays bounded no matter how many tool calls a turn makes.
  • Delta-journal saves. Checkpoints append only what changed to a sidecar <session>.delta.jsonl journal instead of rewriting the whole session JSON, so saving stays fast at any transcript length. The journal folds back into the canonical file when the session closes.
  • Auto-compaction. When the model context approaches its window, the TUI warns once and then compacts automatically before the next request; a mid-turn overflow is self-healed by the provider SDKs. /compact remains available for manual runs.
  • Persistent input history. Submitted prompts are kept in ~/.openmed/history.jsonl (capped, local-only, skipped in DEID mode) so Up/Down recall works across restarts.

docs.title: Plans, tools, and workflow cards
docs.text:
When the agent decides on a multi-step path, it records a plan in the chat and advances it as tools complete.

OpenMed has two planning layers:

  • The visible phase plan is the compact checklist shown in the TUI. It is optimized for the current few steps.
  • The durable global plan is a Markdown/JSON ledger for long tasks with many requirements or deliverables. It is stored in the workspace or workflow output directory and is checked before the agent claims the full task is complete.

By default, repository-scoped ledgers are written to ./.openmed/OPENMED_PLAN.md and ./.openmed/OPENMED_PLAN.json. Workflow/output-scoped ledgers are written beside the generated artifacts as OPENMED_PLAN.md and OPENMED_PLAN.json.

Tool execution shows up inline with start/end states. Deterministic workflows can also emit cards of these types:

  • info
  • evidence
  • suggestion
  • uncertainty

Cards are part of the persisted session history and replay when you reopen the session.

Workflow tool receipts can also include recommended_skills and skill_hint. These fields are operator-facing guidance for loading companion overlays such as citing-evidence, handling-phi-disclosure, escalating-to-reviewer, or preparing-clinical-artifacts before summarizing, packaging, or finalizing a workflow result.

docs.title: Review surfaces
docs.text:
There are three different review surfaces to understand:

  1. The inline conversation itself: plans, tool calls, results, and cards stay visible
  2. Deterministic workflows: draft previews can be inspected before finalization. The returned approval_token validates the workflow request parameters but is not authorization. The reviewed cards, evidence, and full artifact bytes are stored in a private, session-owned immutable snapshot identified by the draft run ID and SHA-256 digest. Snapshots expire after 24 hours by default and are removed after successful finalization, session clear/rollback, or session deletion; /drafts hides expired or missing snapshots and shows the expiry time for active ones. Missing, altered, expired, mismatched, or ambiguously selected snapshots fail closed. Reviewer-gated workflows also require review_metadata captured by the UI.

Finalized bundles are staged and committed atomically. The destination must be new, empty, or an existing OpenMed-owned bundle for the same workflow; filesystem roots, mount points, the live working directory, session state, and arbitrary nonempty directories are rejected before a draft becomes finalizable.

Delivery intent is request-scoped. If the user asks for finalized output, the app creates the immutable draft first and then finalizes that exact snapshot at turn settle. If the user asks for a draft, or does not name a delivery state, the draft is the completed result and the plan ends normally. A later message such as “looks good, send it” is interpreted by a small auxiliary model on your configured provider and mapped to the active draft without asking for a run ID. Questions, edits, negations, classifier failures, and ambiguous targets never finalize. Reviewer-gated workflows open the reviewer-metadata form only when the final write is actually due.

  1. Approval-gated tools: in Ask mode, edit_file and any tool matching ask_tools pause for an approval dialog on every provider. The dialog offers Allow Once, Always This Session, and Deny

Do not assume every tool pauses for approval. write_file and the export tools run without a prompt unless you list them in ask_tools. Workflow delivery does not pause the plan: the host interprets delivery intent, while every draft_only=false call still requires the ephemeral one-use grant plus the verified immutable snapshot selected outside the agent model.

docs.title: Slash commands
docs.text: Command Behavior /clear Clear the conversation and its context /help Open help /model Open the model picker /skill Open the skill switcher /agent Open the agent-mode switcher /access Open the access-mode switcher /session Open the session switcher /theme Open the theme picker /phi Cycle the PHI mode: full, deid, strict. Changing it resets the provider session and drops queued messages /privacy Review clinical file redaction and save output; see Clinical NLP /privacy-batch Run or resume clinical privacy across a file /privacy-chat [off\|on\|auto] Set file privacy; with no argument, turn it on /autoapprove [on\|off] Toggle unattended auto-approval of tool prompts (each bypass is logged; workflow snapshot and reviewer safeguards are never bypassed; also openmed --auto-approve or OPENMED_AUTO_APPROVE=1 for scripted demos/tests) /copy [n] Copy the newest message's last fenced code block to the clipboard (/copy n picks the nth); copies the original text, not the wrapped rendering. Selecting any text with the mouse also auto-copies it. /plan Show the visible phase plan and global plan summary /plan global Show the durable global plan summary /plan pending Show pending or invalid global plan tasks /plan open Print the Markdown and JSON global plan paths /compact Compact older context /compact thinking Remove thinking blocks only /fork [n] Fork the current session, optionally at message n /rollback N Undo the last N user turns /undo Undo the last user turn /retry Re-send the last user prompt /mcp Show MCP server status /workflows List deterministic workflows and required inputs /drafts List active workflow drafts and human-readable destinations; ask naturally to finalize one /finalize [draft] Finalize a reviewed draft. If a turn is running, the finalize is queued until it ends /config Show effective runtime configuration — permission mode, allow/deny/ask rules, project root, loaded settings sources, and persistence threshold /audit Show audit status, destination, PHI payload mode, fallback path, and audit CLI commands /reset Reset agent state

Type $ or use /skill to browse built-in and user-provided skills.

docs.title: Native tools, web search, and MCP
docs.text:
The default registry includes more than 90 native tools. On OpenAI and ChatGPT sign-in, setting OPENMED_BUILTIN_WEB_SEARCH=1 also exposes the provider's built-in web_search, which is separate from the registered native tools.

Those native tools cover:

  • file and artifact operations
  • extraction and PII tooling
  • consumer health imports and analysis
  • PubMed
  • ICD-10, CPT, SNOMED, LOINC, RxNorm, MedlinePlus, HCC, RAF, and crosswalks
  • workflow orchestration
  • planning and skill loading

Many of the medical tools use OpenMed's native medical service plane. They are still native OpenMed tools from the model's perspective, not MCP tools.

MCP remains optional. Use # or /mcp when you want to bring in external systems that are not already part of the native tool surface.

The consumer-import and care-coordination adapter paths are local-only review flows. OpenMed does not auto-send patient messages or write back into external systems from those lanes.

docs.title: OPENMED.md
docs.text: Drop an OPENMED.md file at your git root (or in the working directory, outside a git repository) to inject per-project instructions into the system prompt. The file is loaded at SDK initialization and appended as a ## Project Instructions (OPENMED.md) section. This is useful for customizing agent behavior per workspace without modifying the built-in prompts.

docs.title: Permission policy
docs.text:
OpenMed supports rule-based permission modes that control how tools are gated before execution:

Mode Behavior auto Tools with requires_approval or is_destructive prompt for approval; others run freely acceptall All tools run without approval unless blocked by a deny rule denyall Tools are blocked unless they match allow_tools or ask_tools plan Only read-only, concurrent-safe tools run, plus any that match allow_tools or ask_tools

Set the mode in .openmed/settings.json at the project root or in ~/.openmed/settings.json for user-level defaults:

{
  "permission_mode": "auto",
  "deny_tools": ["edit_*"],
  "ask_tools": ["write_file"]
}

deny_tools removes matching tools entirely, and ask_tools makes matching tools prompt. allow_tools is a strict allowlist: when it is set, the model sees only the matching tools, and they run without a prompt. See Runtime Settings.

The access mode you select in the TUI takes priority over a stored permission_mode, except for Ask, which uses the stored mode. Settings cascade: CLI arguments take highest priority, then project settings, then user settings.

Use /config in the TUI to see the effective runtime configuration at any time.

docs.title: Tool safety classification
docs.text:
Every registered tool carries safety metadata:

  • is_read_only — tool does not modify state
  • is_concurrent_safe — tool can run in parallel with others
  • is_destructive — tool may cause data loss

The permission policy reads these flags, and OpenMed runs a turn's read-only, concurrent-safe tool calls in parallel.

docs.title: Oversized tool result persistence
docs.text:
When a tool produces output exceeding the configured threshold (default 50,000 characters), the result is automatically written to disk. The model receives a compact stub with the file path, size, content type, and a 500-character preview, plus a hint to use read_file for the full content. Configure the threshold in project or user settings:

{
  "tool_result_persist_threshold_chars": 50000
}

docs.title: Web Search
docs.text: OpenMed does not search the web unless you turn it on — on every provider, including OpenAI and ChatGPT OAuth. This page explains why, what enabling it sends where, and how to configure it.

docs.title: Why it is off by default
docs.text:
A search query built from a case tends to contain clinical detail. Sending that query to a hosted search API makes that vendor a third-party data processor for your patient data. That is a decision an operator should make deliberately, with knowledge of which vendor and under which agreement — not one inherited from a default.

There is a second reason, specific to clinical work. OpenAI's Responses API can run a provider-side search where the model searches and returns prose. Those results never reach OpenMed as inspectable sources, so a claim drawn from them cannot be traced back to a page you can open and check. OpenMed's evidence rules require citations to be verifiable, so OpenMed does not request provider-side search unless you opt in separately; see provider-native search. The search on this page runs client-side, and every result becomes a source record with a URL you can inspect.

docs.title: What still works with search off
docs.text:
Search being off does not mean OpenMed is cut off from evidence:

  • PubMed, MedlinePlus and RxNorm lookups work normally and do not use a third-party search vendor. Those queries go from your machine to the public APIs, so avoid identifiers in them.
  • fetch_web_page retrieves a specific URL you or the agent already has.
  • The literature and guideline workflows are unaffected.

What is unavailable is open-ended discovery — "find me recent papers on X" where no URL is known yet.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
Two things are required: the feature flag, and a backend key. A key on its own does nothing, so that adding a key for another purpose can never silently start sending clinical text to a vendor.

export OPENMED_WEB_SEARCH=1
export SERPER_API_KEY="..."

The flag accepts 1, true, yes or on. Restart OpenMed after changing it.

Supported backends:

Backend Key Sign-up Serper SERPER_API_KEY https://serper.dev Tavily TAVILY_API_KEY https://tavily.com Brave Search BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY https://brave.com/search/api/

With more than one key present, OpenMed picks the first configured backend in the order above. To pin one explicitly:

export OPENMED_WEB_SEARCH_BACKEND=tavily

Keys can also live in ~/.openmed/service_secrets.json rather than the environment. Each backend has its own top-level field:

{
  "web_search_serper_api_key": "...",
  "web_search_tavily_api_key": "...",
  "web_search_brave_api_key": "..."
}

Include only the backends you use. A value can be "{env:NAME}" to read it from the environment variable NAME.

Keys are sent as request headers, not as query parameters, so they do not appear in request URLs. They are not embedded in the binary, and openmed env does not print them.

docs.title: Checking the state
docs.text:
openmed env

reports whether search is enabled and which backend is active. When the flag is set but no usable backend is found, the search tool stays available and tells the model what is missing, so it can tell you what to do. Without the flag, the tool is not offered to the model at all.

docs.title: What gets sent
docs.text:
When enabled, the search query goes to the backend you configured. The query is composed by the model from the conversation, so assume it can contain clinical detail. The rest of the case is not sent.

Search results come back as titles, URLs and snippets. Snippets are the search engine's summaries, not page content. The agent is instructed to fetch a page with fetch_web_page before citing anything from it.

PHI and third-party search

If you handle PHI under HIPAA or equivalent, treat a search vendor as a sub-processor. Confirm your agreement covers it before enabling search on sessions that touch patient data, or keep search off and rely on the PubMed and guideline tools, which do not use one.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
unset OPENMED_WEB_SEARCH

After a restart, the search tool is not offered to the model.
